questions.title: Five notification systems
questions.prompt: Five product teams have each built their own system for sending emails, push notifications and text messages. Leadership asks whether there should be one notification platform. What do you recommend, and what would it include?
hints: What problems do the five systems share — and where do they differ for good reasons?
What should the platform own, and what should stay with product teams?
What is the cost of doing nothing?
followups: One team's system is far better than the others. Build on it or start fresh?
How do you avoid becoming a bottleneck for every product team?
What would make you decide not to build it?
criteria: Finds the shared problems (deliverability, preferences, rate limits, compliance).
Leaves content and timing decisions with product teams.
Considers building on the best existing system.
Designs for self-service to avoid bottlenecks.
Quantifies the case (duplicated cost, incidents, user complaints).
outline: Shared pains: user preferences and unsubscribes, quiet hours, frequency caps across teams, provider failover, compliance.
Team-specific: content, triggers, targeting.
Scope: delivery, preferences, global frequency caps, templates, analytics.
Start: extend the best existing system; migrate others gradually.
Self-service: APIs, template tools, documentation.
Case: duplicated engineering, deliverability incidents, users overwhelmed by uncoordinated messages.
questions.reference:
Yes, but a narrow one. The five systems share problems product teams should not solve five times: respecting user preferences and unsubscribes, quiet hours, a global cap so users are not flooded by five teams at once, failover between providers, deliverability and legal compliance. Those belong in the platform. What each message says, when it triggers and whom it targets stay with the product teams.

I would build on the best existing system if its design is sound, rather than start fresh, and migrate other teams gradually. To avoid becoming a bottleneck, everything is self-service: an API, a template tool and clear documentation; the platform team does not review every message.

The case: engineering time spent maintaining five systems, deliverability incidents, and complaints from users receiving uncoordinated messages. If teams’ needs turned out to be genuinely different and the overlap small, I would instead publish shared libraries and standards.

questions.title: Teams are building around you
questions.prompt: You own the internal deployment platform. Several teams have quietly built their own deployment scripts instead of using it. What do you do?
hints: Why did they build their own?
What would make the platform the easiest choice?
followups: One team says the platform is too slow for their release cadence. What now?
How do you publish your roadmap to internal customers?
criteria: Treats workarounds as user research.
Segments teams by need.
Fixes the highest-impact gaps.
Creates clear intake, roadmap and support channels.
Avoids mandates until the platform is clearly better.
outline: Interview teams that built workarounds: what was missing.
Segment: speed-focused, compliance-heavy, simple services.
Fix: top gaps (speed, flexibility hooks, documentation).
Engage: roadmap, office hours, intake.
Measure: share of deploys on platform, deploy time, satisfaction.
Mandate only for security or compliance needs, with support.
questions.reference:
Workarounds are the best user research available: each one shows what the platform failed to provide. I would interview those teams and look at their scripts. Common reasons: the platform is slow, cannot handle a special case, or is hard to understand.

Then segment: teams that need fast, frequent releases; teams with heavy compliance needs; simple services. I would fix the gaps that matter most to the most teams — often deploy speed and extension points that let teams add their own steps safely.

I would run the platform like a product: a published roadmap, an intake process, office hours and a feedback channel. Success is the share of deployments on the platform, deploy time and team satisfaction. I would avoid mandating until the platform is clearly better — except for security requirements, where a mandate comes with migration help.
pitfalls: Blaming teams for not using the platform.

questions.title: Proving a platform's value
questions.prompt: The CFO asks what the company gets for the forty engineers on your internal data platform. How do you measure and show its value?
hints: What would teams do without the platform?
Which outcomes of other teams does the platform change?
Which numbers would a CFO believe?
followups: Usage is high but teams still complain. What does that tell you?
How do you avoid vanity metrics like 'tables created'?
What would you cut if the team shrank by a quarter?
criteria: Measures outcomes for consuming teams (time to insight, reliability).
Estimates cost avoided versus alternatives.
Includes adoption and satisfaction.
Avoids vanity metrics.
Communicates in finance terms.
outline: Outcomes: time from question to answer; pipeline reliability; incidents avoided.
Cost: compute cost per query trend; duplicated tooling avoided.
Adoption: share of teams and workloads on platform.
Satisfaction: quarterly survey, support load.
Story: what teams achieved because of the platform.
questions.reference:
I would measure the platform through the teams that use it. Outcomes: how long it takes an analyst to answer a new question, how reliable critical pipelines are, how many data incidents reach decision-makers. Costs: compute cost per workload over time, and what teams would otherwise spend building and running their own tools.

Adoption and satisfaction complete the picture: share of teams and workloads on the platform, a short quarterly survey, support load. For the CFO, I would translate into money — engineer time saved across consuming teams, infrastructure savings, incidents avoided — with honest ranges, plus two or three concrete stories of decisions the platform made possible.

I would not report tables created or jobs run; those grow whether or not the platform creates value.

questions.title: Turning off the old cluster
questions.prompt: Your company has a new compute platform, but 200 services still run on the old one, which is expensive and has security problems. Plan the migration so the old platform is actually switched off.
hints: Why have the 200 services not moved yet?
Which services are easy and which hard?
How do you keep migration from stalling at 90%?
followups: Teams say they have no time this quarter. What do you do?
The last ten services belong to a team that was disbanded. Who migrates them?
How do you report progress to leadership?
criteria: Understands blockers; makes migration easy (tooling, guides, doing early ones).
Segments services by difficulty and value.
Sets a timeline with leadership support.
Handles orphaned services.
Tracks progress publicly and turns the old platform off.
outline: Blockers survey: missing features, effort, risk.
Close gaps in the new platform first.
Tooling: automated migration for standard services.
Waves: easy services first; platform team migrates a few itself.
Timeline with executive sponsor; capacity reserved in team plans.
Orphans: platform team or an assigned owner.
Public dashboard; final shutdown date; brownouts.
questions.reference:
I would find out why the 200 services have not moved: missing features in the new platform, migration effort, or fear of risk. Missing features get fixed first — otherwise every conversation stalls.

Then make migrating cheap: automated tooling for standard services, a step-by-step guide, and the platform team migrating the first few itself to prove the path. Services are grouped into waves, easy ones first, to build momentum and learn.

An executive sponsor agrees the timeline, and migration time is reserved in team plans, so ‘no time this quarter’ is not an answer. Orphaned services — whose team no longer exists — are assigned an owner or migrated by the platform team.

Progress is shown on a public dashboard by team. As the end approaches, scheduled brownouts reveal forgotten dependencies, and on the shutdown date the old platform is actually switched off. The last 10% needs the most attention — I would plan for it from the start.

questions.title: A team that did not have to listen
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time you persuaded a team that did not report to you to adopt something you built.
hints: What did you change in your product?
followups: What did you learn about their needs?
Would you do it the same way again?
criteria: Understood the team's reluctance.
Changed the product, not just the pitch.
Made adoption easy.
Specific result.
Lesson about internal customers.
outline: What you built and the team.
Their concerns.
What you changed.
How you helped them adopt.
Result.
Lesson.
questions.reference: A strong answer (a model of structure, not a script): “Our search team refused our shared feature store because it added latency. Instead of arguing, I asked for their latency budget and their worst queries. We added a low-latency read path and paired one of our engineers with them for two weeks. They migrated their main model, latency stayed within budget, and they later contributed a caching improvement back. I learned to treat refusals as requirements.”
